newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN OPPOSITION PRESSES ON WITH PROTESTS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN OPPOSITION PRESSES ON WITH PROTESTS.

text.p: Bulgarian students and opposition parties plan a 26th day of nationwide anti-government protests on Friday after rejecting a compromise offer on early elections by the embattled ruling socialists.
Supporters of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) cut road and rail links at many points around the Balkan country and staged mass rallies in a dozen towns on Thursday.

"It is obvious that since the UDF stepped up the protests, the Socialists' chances of forming a second government are decreasing every minute," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told a mass rally in the capital.
President Petar Stoyanov returns on Friday from a visit to the European Union headquarters in Brussels, where he bluntly said Bulgaria may default on its $10 billion foreign debt.

Before leaving he gave the Socialists a mandate to try to form a government, which must then be approved by parliament. The Socialists have overseen a caretaker cabinet since prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who is struggling to form a cabinet in the face of widespread popular opposition, said he would serve only three to five months and then hold elections.
But that compromise offer failed to placate the opposition, which wants elections now, and protests were intensified around the country on Thursday.

Protesters blocked main roads to Greece and Turkey, strikes hit schools, factories and mines, and public transport in the second city of Plovdiv ran only to carry people to the daily opposition rally.
Sofia students marched through the city bound in ropes, to symbolise they were no better than slaves, and then danced and frolicked on the main Eagles' Bridge -- causing traffic chaos.
Thousands of UDF supporters marched through the capital in a separate demonstration on Thursday, blowing whistles, beating drums and chanting for the government quit.
Many protesters carried the white, green and red Bulgarian flag upside down to symbolise a nation in distress. One banner proclaimed "Bulgaria should not be Burundi".
The Socialists, formerly the communists, won elections in December 1994 but have struggled to stay in power for several months as the economy has collapsed.
The lev has hit record lows daily against the dollar and inflation is forecast to reach 50 percent in January alone. Bulgarians have seen their wages and savings plummet in real terms.
Dobrev must submit his cabinet to a vote in the 240-seat parliament by Tuesday. He has an absolute majority but the UDF is trying to woo enough defections to stop him.
The challenge to the government has been mostly peaceful but the UDF warned supporters on Thursday that the Socialists could try to provoke clashes.

The Socialists' youth wing had planned a counter-rally on Friday. One organiser said it had been cancelled after Sofia's UDF mayor set limitations on the route, but the UDF said that it expected the rally to go ahead.

"We have heard that 100 buses will bring about 5,000 Socialist supporters to Sofia," Kostov told the Sofia rally. "Everyone understands that they are clearly looking for a clash but we shall not allow this to happen."
In another sign of collapse, the state gas firm Bulgargas said it was reducing supplies to several big industrial clients who had not paid their bills.
